passages.t: Solomon's officials and the twelve districts
passages.happening:
‘So King Solomon ruled over Israel’ (verse 1), and the chapter lists his chief officials: priests, secretaries, a recorder, the commander of the army, a man in charge of the governors, an adviser to the king, a man in charge of the palace, ‘and Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labor’ (verse 6).

Then come twelve governors over all Israel to provide food for the king and his household. ‘Each one would arrange provisions for one month of the year’ (verse 7). The list names them and their districts, from the hill country of Ephraim to Naphtali, Asher, Issachar and Benjamin, and east of the Jordan to Gilead and Bashan. Two of the governors are married to Solomon's daughters (verses 11, 15). The list ends with a short note: “There was also one governor in the land of Judah” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
Lists like these were probably drawn from royal records. This one shows a court more developed than David's. Several officials are sons of David's officials, the start of a class of men who ran the kingdom for the king. Adoniram, over the forced labor, is likely the Adoram of David's last years. And Abiathar appears among the priests, though he was sent away in chapter 2, which suggests that the list comes from early in the reign or keeps his title.

The twelve districts do not simply follow the old tribal borders. Some carry a tribe's name; others are named for regions and towns, among them old Canaanite centers such as Megiddo, Taanach and Beth-shean. Many historians see a deliberate reorganization for taxation. Each district fed the court for one month a year.

Whether Judah was spared that burden is debated. The last line mentions one governor in the land of Judah. Some read it as a separate arrangement for the king's own tribe; others as a thirteenth official. Any sense that Judah was favored would help explain the north's anger when it breaks away in chapter 12.
passages.later: David's own officials are listed in 2 Samuel, with the same man over the same work: ‘Adoram was in charge of the forced labor’ (2 Samuel 20:24).
passages.asks: Solomon's kingdom ran on lists, districts and quotas, and on the forced labor of his people. Ask who carries the cost of the order and comfort you enjoy. And ask whether the systems you help to run treat people fairly, or treat some as more favored than others.

passages.happening:
“The people of Judah and Israel were as numerous as the sand on the seashore, and they were eating and drinking and rejoicing” (verse 20). Solomon reigns over the kingdoms from the Euphrates to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt, and they bring him tribute (verse 21).

The palace's food for a single day is listed: thirty cors of fine flour and sixty of meal, ten fat oxen and twenty range oxen, a hundred sheep, with deer, gazelles, roebucks and fattened poultry (verses 22-23). Solomon has peace on all sides (verse 24). “Throughout the days of Solomon, Judah and Israel dwelt securely from Dan to Beersheba, each man under his own vine and his own fig tree” (verse 25).

He has ‘4,000 stalls for his chariot horses and 12,000 horses’ (verse 26). The governors take turns supplying his table, and barley and straw for his horses. ‘They saw to it that nothing was lacking’ (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
This is the high point of Israel's life in the land, and its words recall God's promises to Abraham: descendants as many as the sand on the seashore, and a land reaching to the Euphrates. Here both are described as fulfilled. The reach to the Euphrates is understood by many historians as a web of tribute and influence rather than direct rule, and the text itself speaks of kingdoms that brought tribute.

The royal table was enormous. A cor was a dry measure, often estimated at about two hundred liters, so the daily flour and meal could feed many thousands: family, officials, guards, servants and guests. Meat was a luxury in Israel, and the list shows a court far beyond ordinary life.

The picture of each man under his own vine and fig tree (verse 25) became Israel's classic image of peace. It meant a family owning its land, eating its own fruit and living without fear of raids.

Yet the careful reader notices what will grow into trouble: a large central court, forced labor, thousands of horses, and a daily demand for food laid on the districts. The golden age already holds the pressures that will split the kingdom.

One number needs a word. Most Hebrew manuscripts of verse 26 read forty thousand stalls. The parallel in Chronicles reads four thousand, and the BSB follows it, as the site's page on the numbers in Samuel, Kings and Chronicles explains.
passages.later:
God had promised Abraham, ‘I will multiply your descendants like the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore’ (Genesis 22:17), and a land reaching ‘from the river of Egypt to the great River Euphrates’ (Genesis 15:18).

The prophet Micah takes up the vine and the fig tree for the peace of God's coming kingdom: “And each man will sit under his own vine and under his own fig tree, with no one to frighten him” (Micah 4:4).
passages.hard:
Was Solomon's kingdom really this large and this rich?

This is a live debate. Some archaeologists, pointing to monumental gates and walls at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer, the three cities linked with Solomon's building in 9:15, argue for a substantial kingdom in the tenth century BC. Others date some of those structures to the ninth century and see Solomon's Jerusalem as a smaller highland capital, with the biblical picture shaped by later memory. Still others take a middle position.

The text itself describes much of Solomon's reach as tribute and influence rather than direct rule. The archaeological picture is incomplete and contested, and the biblical writer's main concern is theological: the promises to Abraham reaching a high point under the son of David. The site's page on what archaeology shows sets out the evidence on both sides.
passages.asks: Israel ate and drank and was glad, each family under its own vine. Ask whether you receive the good things in your life as gifts, or as what you are owed. And ask what it costs other people to keep your table full.

passages.t: Wisdom like the sand on the seashore
passages.happening:
“And God gave Solomon wisdom, exceedingly deep insight, and understanding beyond measure, like the sand on the seashore” (verse 29). His wisdom is greater than that of all the men of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt, greater than that of Ethan the Ezrahite and of Heman, Calcol and Darda (verses 30-31).

“Solomon composed three thousand proverbs, and his songs numbered a thousand and five” (verse 32). He spoke of trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop growing in the wall, and he taught about animals, birds, reptiles and fish (verse 33). People came from every nation to listen, sent by kings who had heard of his wisdom (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Wisdom in the ancient world was an international pursuit. Egypt had its collections of instruction, such as the Instruction of Amenemope, and Mesopotamia its proverbs and wisdom texts. The men of the East probably means the peoples of the Syrian and Arabian desert, known for wisdom; Job is described as a man of the East. To say that Solomon surpassed them all is to say that Israel's king excelled in the most admired learning of his day.

Ethan the Ezrahite and Heman are names known elsewhere. The headings of Psalms 89 and 88 name them, and Chronicles names singers called Heman and Ethan in David's day. Whether these are the same men is not known.

Solomon's wisdom took in the natural world. Listing and watching trees and creatures was a way of learning how the world works. The word for his proverbs, mashal, covers short sayings, comparisons and parables. The book of Proverbs, whose title uses the word, is linked with Solomon, though it also holds collections by others.

Sand appears twice in the chapter, for the people's number (verse 20) and for the king's understanding (verse 29). The nation's flourishing and the king's wisdom are set side by side.

In Hebrew Bibles verses 21 to 34 of this chapter are numbered as 5:1-14, so the chapter and verse numbers differ there between Hebrew and English Bibles.
passages.later:
The book of Proverbs opens with his name: ‘These are the proverbs of Solomon son of David, king of Israel’ (Proverbs 1:1). It learns from creatures as he did: “Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise” (Proverbs 6:6).

Jesus pointed to the wildflowers of Galilee and said that ‘not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these’ (Matthew 6:29).
passages.asks: Solomon's learning reached from the cedar to the hyssop on the wall. Ask whether you treat the ordinary world as a place where God can teach you. And ask what you most want to understand, and why.
